csp.missing.title: No Content-Security-Policy header
csp.missing.why: Without a CSP the browser will execute any script the page references or injects, so any HTML injection becomes script execution. CSP is the only defence-in-depth layer that survives a templating mistake.

csp.present.title: Content-Security-Policy is set
csp.present.why: A Content-Security-Policy header is enforced by the browser.

csp.report-only-only.title: Only Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only is set
csp.report-only-only.why: Report-Only never blocks anything. It is a rollout tool, not a control: an attacker's injected script runs exactly as it would with no policy at all.

csp.report-only-present.title: A Report-Only policy is deployed alongside the enforced one
csp.report-only-present.why: Running a stricter policy in report-only mode next to the enforced one is the recommended way to tighten CSP safely.

csp.multiple-policies.title: Multiple Content-Security-Policy headers are sent
csp.multiple-policies.why: Multiple policies are intersected by the browser, so the result is at least as strict as each one. It is usually accidental (a proxy or CDN adding its own) and makes the effective policy hard to reason about.

csp.parse-error.title: Content-Security-Policy contains unknown or malformed directives
csp.parse-error.why: Browsers ignore directives they do not understand. A typo silently removes the protection you thought you had deployed.

csp.deprecated-directive.title: Content-Security-Policy uses deprecated directives
csp.deprecated-directive.why: Deprecated directives such as block-all-mixed-content or referrer are ignored by current browsers and give a false sense of coverage.

csp.default-src.missing.title: CSP has no default-src fallback
csp.default-src.missing.why: Fetch directives you did not list fall back to default-src. Without it, connect-src, font-src, frame-src, worker-src and friends are completely unrestricted.

csp.default-src.permissive.title: CSP default-src is permissive
csp.default-src.permissive.why: A default-src of * or https: does not restrict anything meaningful for the directives that fall back to it.

csp.default-src.ok.title: CSP declares a restrictive default-src
csp.default-src.ok.why: Directives that are not listed explicitly fall back to a restrictive default.

csp.script-src.unsafe-inline.title: script-src allows 'unsafe-inline'
csp.script-src.unsafe-inline.why: 'unsafe-inline' with no nonce or hash present lets any injected <script> tag or inline event handler run. This is the single change that most often reduces a CSP to decoration.

csp.script-src.unsafe-inline-ignored.title: script-src has 'unsafe-inline' but a nonce or hash is present
csp.script-src.unsafe-inline-ignored.why: CSP3 browsers ignore 'unsafe-inline' when a nonce or hash source is present, so it only affects CSP1 browsers. Keeping it is the documented backwards-compatibility pattern.

csp.script-src.unsafe-eval.title: script-src allows 'unsafe-eval'
csp.script-src.unsafe-eval.why: 'unsafe-eval' re-enables eval(), new Function() and string timers, which turns many DOM-based sinks back into script execution even when source restrictions hold.

csp.script-src.wildcard.title: script-src allows a wildcard source
csp.script-src.wildcard.why: A source of *, https: or http: lets scripts load from any host on the internet, so an attacker only needs to be able to inject a <script src> tag.

csp.script-src.data-uri.title: script-src allows data: URIs
csp.script-src.data-uri.why: data: in script-src means the attacker supplies the script body inline in the URL. It defeats the whole source allowlist.

csp.script-src.bypassable-host.title: script-src allows a host known to be CSP-bypassable
csp.script-src.bypassable-host.why: Some popular CDNs host JSONP endpoints, AngularJS or unrestricted user content. Allowlisting them lets an attacker load attacker-controlled JavaScript from a host your policy trusts.

csp.script-src.missing.title: CSP restricts nothing for scripts
csp.script-src.missing.why: Neither script-src nor default-src is present, so script loading is unrestricted.

csp.script-src.strict-dynamic.title: script-src uses 'strict-dynamic' with nonces or hashes
csp.script-src.strict-dynamic.why: This is the recommended modern shape: trust propagates from nonced scripts to the scripts they load, and host allowlists (and their bypasses) stop mattering.

csp.script-src.ok.title: script-src is restrictive
csp.script-src.ok.why: Script sources are limited to an explicit allowlist with no inline execution.

csp.style-src.unsafe-inline.title: style-src allows 'unsafe-inline'
csp.style-src.unsafe-inline.why: Inline styles enable CSS-based data exfiltration and UI redressing. It is much less severe than inline script and is often impractical to remove, but it is not free.

csp.style-src.missing.title: CSP restricts nothing for stylesheets
csp.style-src.missing.why: Neither style-src nor default-src is present, so stylesheet loading and inline styles are unrestricted.

csp.style-src.ok.title: style-src is restrictive
csp.style-src.ok.why: Stylesheets are limited to an explicit allowlist with no inline styles.

csp.object-src.missing.title: CSP does not set object-src 'none'
csp.object-src.missing.why: Legacy plugin content (<object>, <embed>) can execute script in some browsers. object-src 'none' is free to deploy and closes that path.

csp.object-src.permissive.title: CSP object-src is permissive
csp.object-src.permissive.why: An object-src that is not 'none' leaves plugin-based script execution reachable. Almost no site needs it.

csp.base-uri.missing.title: CSP does not set base-uri
csp.base-uri.missing.why: base-uri does not fall back to default-src. Without it an injected <base> tag rewrites every relative script URL on the page, which bypasses a host allowlist entirely.

csp.base-uri.permissive.title: CSP base-uri is permissive
csp.base-uri.permissive.why: A wildcard base-uri leaves the injected-<base> bypass open.

csp.base-uri.ok.title: CSP sets a restrictive base-uri
csp.base-uri.ok.why: Injected <base> tags cannot redirect relative script URLs.

csp.frame-ancestors.missing.title: CSP does not set frame-ancestors
csp.frame-ancestors.missing.why: frame-ancestors is the modern clickjacking control and does not fall back to default-src. Without it (and without X-Frame-Options) the page can be framed by anyone.

csp.frame-ancestors.permissive.title: CSP frame-ancestors allows any origin
csp.frame-ancestors.permissive.why: frame-ancestors * explicitly permits framing from anywhere, which is a clickjacking primitive.

csp.frame-ancestors.ok.title: CSP sets a restrictive frame-ancestors
csp.frame-ancestors.ok.why: Framing is limited to an explicit set of origins.

csp.reporting.uri-without-to.title: CSP uses report-uri without report-to
csp.reporting.uri-without-to.why: report-uri is deprecated and is being removed from Chromium. Without a matching report-to and Reporting-Endpoints header you will stop receiving violation reports.

hsts.missing.title: No Strict-Transport-Security header
hsts.missing.why: Without HSTS the first request of every session can be downgraded to plain HTTP by an on-path attacker, and the redirect to HTTPS happens too late to protect the cookies already sent.

hsts.malformed.title: Strict-Transport-Security is malformed
hsts.malformed.why: A header the browser cannot parse (missing or non-numeric max-age) is discarded, so the site behaves as if HSTS were never deployed.

hsts.max-age-zero.title: Strict-Transport-Security has max-age=0
hsts.max-age-zero.why: max-age=0 actively tells browsers to forget the HSTS entry for this host. It is the documented way to turn HSTS off.

hsts.max-age-low.title: Strict-Transport-Security max-age is below 180 days
hsts.max-age-low.why: A short max-age shrinks the window in which a returning visitor is protected, and 31536000 (one year) is required for the preload list.

hsts.no-subdomains.title: Strict-Transport-Security lacks includeSubDomains
hsts.no-subdomains.why: Without includeSubDomains an attacker can serve plain HTTP on any subdomain and set cookies scoped to the parent domain, which undermines the protected origin.

hsts.no-preload.title: Strict-Transport-Security lacks preload
hsts.no-preload.why: Preloading removes the trust-on-first-use gap entirely. It is a deliberate, hard-to-reverse commitment, so its absence is reported but not penalised.

hsts.preloaded.title: Domain is on the Chrome HSTS preload list
hsts.preloaded.why: Browsers refuse plain HTTP for this host before the first request is ever made.

hsts.ok.title: Strict-Transport-Security is correctly configured
hsts.ok.why: A long max-age with includeSubDomains is enforced.

hsts.over-http.title: Strict-Transport-Security sent over plain HTTP
hsts.over-http.why: Browsers must ignore HSTS headers received over a non-secure transport. Emitting it there is harmless but signals the header is set globally rather than on the TLS vhost.

xfo.missing.title: No X-Frame-Options header
xfo.missing.why: With neither X-Frame-Options nor CSP frame-ancestors the page can be framed by any site, which enables clickjacking.

xfo.redundant.title: X-Frame-Options is redundant given CSP frame-ancestors
xfo.redundant.why: Every browser that supports frame-ancestors ignores X-Frame-Options when both are present. Keeping it only helps very old clients; it is not a finding.

xfo.invalid.title: X-Frame-Options has an invalid value
xfo.invalid.why: ALLOW-FROM was never implemented outside Firefox and is now removed; any unrecognised value makes browsers fall back to allowing framing.

xfo.allowall.title: X-Frame-Options explicitly allows framing
xfo.allowall.why: The page opts out of framing protection, so a hostile site can overlay it and harvest clicks.

xfo.ok.title: X-Frame-Options denies framing
xfo.ok.why: Legacy clients are protected from clickjacking.

nosniff.missing.title: No X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
nosniff.missing.why: Without nosniff, browsers may MIME-sniff a user-uploaded file as HTML or JavaScript and execute it in your origin. It also enables cross-origin script inclusion of JSON endpoints.

nosniff.invalid.title: X-Content-Type-Options has an unexpected value
nosniff.invalid.why: nosniff is the only defined value. Anything else is ignored and provides no protection.

referrer-policy.missing.title: No Referrer-Policy header
referrer-policy.missing.why: Browser defaults differ. Where the default is still no-referrer-when-downgrade, the full URL of your page, including any tokens in the path or query, is sent to every third-party host you reference.

referrer-policy.leaky.title: Referrer-Policy leaks the full URL to third parties
referrer-policy.leaky.why: unsafe-url and no-referrer-when-downgrade send path and query to cross-origin destinations. Password-reset links, invite tokens and search terms end up in other people's logs.

referrer-policy.unknown.title: Referrer-Policy value is not recognised
referrer-policy.unknown.why: An unknown token is ignored and the browser default applies, so the header does nothing.

referrer-policy.ok.title: Referrer-Policy restricts cross-origin referrers
referrer-policy.ok.why: Third parties receive at most the origin, never the full URL.

permissions-policy.missing.title: No Permissions-Policy header
permissions-policy.missing.why: Powerful features stay available to the document and, in some cases, to embedded third-party frames. Denying what you do not use limits what injected or embedded code can reach.

permissions-policy.open-features.title: Permissions-Policy leaves powerful features open
permissions-policy.open-features.why: Features the policy does not name keep their default allowlist. Camera, microphone, geolocation and payment are worth denying explicitly.

permissions-policy.legacy-feature-policy.title: Legacy Feature-Policy header in use
permissions-policy.legacy-feature-policy.why: Feature-Policy was renamed to Permissions-Policy and uses a different syntax. Current browsers only read the new header.

permissions-policy.ok.title: Permissions-Policy denies the high-risk features
permissions-policy.ok.why: Camera, microphone, geolocation and payment are switched off for this document.

coop.missing.title: No Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header
coop.missing.why: Without COOP a page you open, or that opens you, keeps a window reference across origins. That reference is the basis of tabnabbing and of several XS-Leaks.

coop.weak.title: Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy is unsafe-none
coop.weak.why: unsafe-none is the default and provides no browsing-context isolation.

coop.ok.title: Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy isolates the browsing context
coop.ok.why: Cross-origin documents cannot hold a usable window reference to this page.

coep.missing.title: No Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy header
coep.missing.why: COEP is only needed if you want crossOriginIsolated (SharedArrayBuffer, precise timers). It breaks third-party embeds that do not opt in, so its absence is reported, not penalised.

coep.ok.title: Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy is set
coep.ok.why: Cross-origin subresources must opt in to being embedded.

isolation.enabled.title: Document is cross-origin isolated
isolation.enabled.why: COOP same-origin plus COEP require-corp means the strongest browser-side isolation is active.

corp.missing.title: No Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header
corp.missing.why: CORP tells the browser who may embed this response. It is the cheapest mitigation for Spectre-style cross-origin leaks of resource contents.

corp.ok.title: Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy is set
corp.ok.why: Embedding of this response by other origins is restricted.

info.server-version.title: Server header discloses a software version
info.server-version.why: A precise version turns your host into a match for a CVE feed. It does not make you exploitable, but it removes the attacker's need to fingerprint.

info.server-present.title: Server header present without a version
info.server-present.why: The product name alone is low-value information. Suppressing it entirely is cheap but optional.

info.x-powered-by.title: X-Powered-By header discloses the application stack
info.x-powered-by.why: X-Powered-By has no function other than advertising your runtime and its version.

info.aspnet-version.title: ASP.NET version headers are exposed
info.aspnet-version.why: X-AspNet-Version and X-AspNetMvc-Version pin the exact framework build in use.

info.x-generator.title: X-Generator header discloses the CMS
info.x-generator.why: Naming the CMS and its version points straight at the matching exploit set.

info.none.title: No version-disclosing headers
info.none.why: The response does not advertise software versions.

legacy.x-xss-protection.title: X-XSS-Protection header is present
legacy.x-xss-protection.why: The XSS auditor was removed from every major browser because its filtering introduced information leaks and could itself be used to disable legitimate scripts. Modern guidance is to send X-XSS-Protection: 0 or nothing at all.

legacy.public-key-pins.title: Public-Key-Pins header is present
legacy.public-key-pins.why: HPKP was withdrawn after repeated incidents where a bad pin bricked a domain for the whole max-age. Browsers ignore it now, but the header is a footgun worth removing.

legacy.expect-ct.title: Expect-CT header is present
legacy.expect-ct.why: Certificate Transparency is now mandatory and enforced unconditionally, so Expect-CT is obsolete and ignored.

legacy.none.title: No deprecated security headers
legacy.none.why: The response carries no withdrawn or counterproductive headers.

cors.wildcard-with-credentials.title: CORS allows any origin together with credentials
cors.wildcard-with-credentials.why: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true is rejected by browsers, but it is a reliable sign the CORS layer is misconfigured, and any server-side variant that echoes the origin instead makes every authenticated response readable by any website the victim visits.

cors.reflects-origin-with-credentials.title: CORS reflects the request Origin and allows credentials
cors.reflects-origin-with-credentials.why: Any site the victim visits can read authenticated responses from this origin, including CSRF tokens and personal data. This is a full cross-origin read of the user's session.

cors.reflects-origin.title: CORS reflects an arbitrary request Origin
cors.reflects-origin.why: Reflecting any origin defeats the point of an allowlist. Without credentials the impact is limited, but it exposes responses that depend on the client IP or on internal network position.

cors.null-origin-allowed.title: CORS allows the null origin
cors.null-origin-allowed.why: Any sandboxed iframe, including one an attacker embeds in their own page, sends Origin: null. Allowing it grants cross-origin read access to anyone.

cors.wildcard.title: CORS allows any origin without credentials
cors.wildcard.why: A wildcard without credentials is the correct configuration for genuinely public resources. Confirm the endpoint really is public.

cors.missing-vary-origin.title: CORS response does not vary on Origin
cors.missing-vary-origin.why: When Access-Control-Allow-Origin depends on the request, a cache without Vary: Origin can hand one origin's allow header to another origin's request.

cors.ok.title: CORS configuration is sound
cors.ok.why: The server does not expose credentialed responses to arbitrary origins.

cookie.no-secure.title: Cookie is missing the Secure flag
cookie.no-secure.why: A cookie without Secure is sent over plain HTTP. One downgraded request, to any path on the host, hands the value to an on-path attacker.

cookie.no-httponly.title: Cookie is missing the HttpOnly flag
cookie.no-httponly.why: Without HttpOnly the cookie is readable from JavaScript, so any XSS turns directly into credential theft.

cookie.session-no-httponly.title: Session-like cookie is missing HttpOnly
cookie.session-no-httponly.why: The cookie name suggests it carries a session or token. Exposing it to JavaScript means any XSS is a full account takeover.

cookie.no-samesite.title: Cookie has no SameSite attribute
cookie.no-samesite.why: Browser defaults differ and some still send the cookie on cross-site top-level POSTs. Setting SameSite explicitly is the only portable behaviour.

cookie.samesite-none-insecure.title: Cookie has SameSite=None without Secure
cookie.samesite-none-insecure.why: SameSite=None requires Secure. Browsers reject the cookie outright, so the combination both breaks the feature and signals the cookie was meant to travel cross-site.

cookie.broad-domain.title: Cookie is scoped to an overly broad domain
cookie.broad-domain.why: A cookie set on the registrable domain is sent to every subdomain, so any one of them, including a forgotten marketing host, can read or overwrite it.

cookie.long-expiry.title: Cookie has a very long lifetime
cookie.long-expiry.why: A multi-year persistent cookie is a long-lived bearer credential if it carries any authentication state.

cookie.prefix-violation.title: Cookie name prefix does not match its attributes
cookie.prefix-violation.why: __Host- and __Secure- prefixes are only honoured when the attributes match. A mismatch means the browser rejects the cookie and the integrity guarantee you thought you had is absent.

cookie.ok.title: Cookies are set with sound attributes
cookie.ok.why: Every cookie carries Secure, HttpOnly where appropriate, and an explicit SameSite.

cookie.none.title: No cookies set on this response

tls.handshake.failed.title: TLS handshake failed for every protocol version
tls.handshake.failed.why: No TLS version tested could complete a handshake, so the host offers no usable HTTPS or blocked the probe.

tls.version.tls10.title: TLS 1.0 is accepted
tls.version.tls10.why: TLS 1.0 has been deprecated by RFC 8996 and is disabled in every current browser. It is vulnerable to BEAST and to downgrade attacks, and it fails PCI DSS.

tls.version.tls11.title: TLS 1.1 is accepted
tls.version.tls11.why: TLS 1.1 is deprecated by RFC 8996 and relies on MD5/SHA-1 in its handshake signatures. No current client needs it.

tls.version.no-tls12.title: TLS 1.2 is not supported
tls.version.no-tls12.why: TLS 1.2 is the compatibility floor for the current web. Without it, clients that do not speak 1.3 cannot connect at all.

tls.version.no-tls13.title: TLS 1.3 is not supported
tls.version.no-tls13.why: TLS 1.3 removes every legacy cipher construction, encrypts more of the handshake and cuts a round trip. Not offering it leaves both security and latency on the table.

tls.version.ok.title: Only modern TLS versions are accepted
tls.version.ok.why: The server speaks TLS 1.2 and/or 1.3 and refuses the deprecated versions.

tls.cipher.insecure.title: Server accepts a broken cipher suite
tls.cipher.insecure.why: RC4, 3DES, NULL, EXPORT and anonymous suites are broken in practice, not just in theory. Accepting one means a determined on-path attacker can read or forge traffic.

tls.cipher.no-forward-secrecy.title: Server accepts cipher suites without forward secrecy
tls.cipher.no-forward-secrecy.why: Static-RSA key exchange means a single future compromise of the private key decrypts every session ever recorded. ECDHE removes that risk.

tls.cipher.cbc.title: Server accepts CBC-mode cipher suites
tls.cipher.cbc.why: CBC with MAC-then-encrypt has produced a decade of padding-oracle and timing attacks (Lucky13 and successors). AEAD suites have no equivalent history.

tls.cipher.client-preference.title: Server follows the client's cipher suite preference
tls.cipher.client-preference.why: When the client picks, a downgraded or hostile client can steer the connection to the weakest mutually supported suite.

tls.cipher.server-preference.title: Server enforces its own cipher suite order
tls.cipher.server-preference.why: The server, not the client, decides which suite is used.

tls.cipher.ok.title: Only strong cipher suites are accepted
tls.cipher.ok.why: All accepted TLS 1.2 suites are AEAD with forward secrecy.

tls.cert.expired.title: Certificate has expired
tls.cert.expired.why: Every browser shows a full-page interstitial. The site is effectively down, and training users to click through such warnings is its own harm.

tls.cert.not-yet-valid.title: Certificate is not yet valid
tls.cert.not-yet-valid.why: The notBefore date is in the future, so clients reject the certificate. Usually a clock or issuance-automation problem.

tls.cert.expiring-soon.title: Certificate expires in less than 30 days
tls.cert.expiring-soon.why: Renewal automation fails quietly more often than it fails loudly. Thirty days is the last point at which a failure is still comfortable to fix.

tls.cert.hostname-mismatch.title: Certificate does not cover the requested hostname
tls.cert.hostname-mismatch.why: No SAN entry matches the host, so clients cannot verify they are talking to the right server. This is indistinguishable from an interception attempt.

tls.cert.self-signed.title: Certificate is self-signed
tls.cert.self-signed.why: A self-signed certificate chains to no trusted root, so it authenticates nothing to a normal client.

tls.cert.untrusted-chain.title: Certificate chain does not verify against the system roots
tls.cert.untrusted-chain.why: Clients will refuse the connection. The cause is usually a missing intermediate, an expired cross-sign, or a private CA.

tls.cert.incomplete-chain.title: Server does not send the full certificate chain
tls.cert.incomplete-chain.why: Browsers often paper over a missing intermediate with AIA fetching or a cached copy. Other clients, including most HTTP libraries and mobile apps, simply fail.

tls.cert.weak-signature.title: Certificate uses a weak signature algorithm
tls.cert.weak-signature.why: SHA-1 and MD5 collisions are practical and have been demonstrated against real certificate issuance. Browsers reject such certificates outright.

tls.cert.weak-key.title: Certificate public key is too small
tls.cert.weak-key.why: RSA below 2048 bits and ECDSA below 256 bits are below the current floor for public trust and are rejected by modern clients.

tls.cert.long-validity.title: Certificate validity period is unusually long
tls.cert.long-validity.why: Long-lived certificates widen the window in which a compromised key stays usable and are no longer issued by public CAs.

tls.cert.no-sct.title: Certificate has no embedded Certificate Transparency SCTs
tls.cert.no-sct.why: Chrome requires CT for publicly trusted certificates. No embedded SCTs means either a private CA or a certificate Chrome will reject.

tls.cert.revoked.title: Certificate is revoked according to OCSP
tls.cert.revoked.why: The issuing CA has withdrawn this certificate, which normally means the key was compromised or mis-issued. It must be replaced immediately.

tls.cert.ok.title: Certificate and chain are valid
tls.cert.ok.why: The chain verifies, the hostname matches and the certificate is well within its validity window.

tls.ocsp.no-stapling.title: OCSP stapling is not enabled
tls.ocsp.no-stapling.why: Without stapling the client either skips revocation checking or leaks which site it is visiting to the CA, and pays a round trip for it.

tls.ocsp.stapled.title: OCSP stapling is enabled
tls.ocsp.stapled.why: The server provides a fresh revocation proof in the handshake.

tls.alpn.no-h2.title: Server does not advertise HTTP/2 over ALPN
tls.alpn.no-h2.why: HTTP/2 is a performance and connection-management improvement rather than a security control, but its absence usually indicates dated server configuration.

tls.alpn.ok.title: Server advertises modern protocols over ALPN

tls.renegotiation.insecure.title: Server does not support secure renegotiation
tls.renegotiation.insecure.why: Without RFC 5746 the server is open to the TLS renegotiation prefix-injection attack, where an attacker prepends their own request to the victim's authenticated session.

tls.compression.enabled.title: TLS compression is enabled
tls.compression.enabled.why: TLS-level compression allows the CRIME attack, which recovers secrets such as session cookies from the compressed ciphertext length.

tls.resumption.none.title: Session resumption is not offered
tls.resumption.none.why: Resumption is a latency optimisation. Disabling it is a defensible trade-off in exchange for simpler forward-secrecy reasoning.

tls.resumption.ok.title: Session resumption is supported
tls.resumption.ok.why: Returning clients can resume without a full handshake.

redirect.no-https.title: Plain HTTP is served without redirecting to HTTPS
redirect.no-https.why: Anything served over HTTP can be read and rewritten in transit. If the same content is reachable over both schemes, an on-path attacker simply keeps the user on the insecure one.

redirect.not-permanent.title: HTTP to HTTPS redirect is not a permanent redirect
redirect.not-permanent.why: A 302 is not cached as a scheme upgrade, so every new visit starts with a plain-HTTP round trip. 301 or 308 is what you want.

redirect.chain-through-http.title: Redirect chain passes through plain HTTP
redirect.chain-through-http.why: A single insecure hop in the middle of the chain exposes cookies and allows the attacker to take over the rest of the navigation, even if the final URL is HTTPS.

redirect.cross-host.title: HTTP redirect goes to a different host
redirect.cross-host.why: Redirecting to a different host in the same hop prevents the browser from recording an HSTS entry for the original host.

redirect.long-chain.title: Redirect chain is unusually long
redirect.long-chain.why: Each hop is a round trip and another chance to drop out of HTTPS or lose the request. Collapse them into one.

redirect.ok.title: HTTP redirects to HTTPS on the same host
redirect.ok.why: Plain HTTP is upgraded immediately and permanently.

mixed-content.active.title: Page references active content over plain HTTP
mixed-content.active.why: A script or iframe loaded over HTTP can be replaced in transit and then runs with full access to the HTTPS origin. Browsers block it, so the feature is also simply broken.

mixed-content.passive.title: Page references passive content over plain HTTP
mixed-content.passive.why: Images and media over HTTP leak the fact of the request and can be swapped by an on-path attacker. Browsers upgrade or block them, which shows up as missing assets.

mixed-content.none.title: No plain-HTTP subresource references found
mixed-content.none.why: The retrieved HTML references no http:// subresources.

security-txt.missing.title: No /.well-known/security.txt
security-txt.missing.why: Without a published contact, someone who finds a vulnerability has to guess where to send it, and often gives up or goes public instead.

security-txt.invalid.title: security.txt does not satisfy RFC 9116
security-txt.invalid.why: Contact and Expires are mandatory fields. A file missing them will be skipped by tooling that consumes it.

security-txt.expired.title: security.txt has expired
security-txt.expired.why: RFC 9116 says an expired file must not be used, so the contact details in it are formally stale.

security-txt.ok.title: Valid security.txt is published
security-txt.ok.why: A reachable, unexpired disclosure contact is published.

methods.trace-enabled.title: TRACE method is enabled
methods.trace-enabled.why: TRACE echoes the request, including headers, back in the body. It has no legitimate production use and historically enabled Cross-Site Tracing.

methods.dangerous-allowed.title: Server advertises write or debug methods
methods.dangerous-allowed.why: PUT, DELETE, CONNECT, PATCH or WebDAV verbs advertised on a static endpoint usually mean a module is enabled that nobody intended to expose.

methods.ok.title: No unexpected HTTP methods advertised
methods.ok.why: Only safe methods are advertised and TRACE is refused.
